slab.e: From Middle English sclabbe, slabbe, of uncertain origin; possibly from *slap, related to dialectal slappel (“portion, piece”), along with slape (“slippery”), sleip (“smooth piece of timber”), borrowed through Old Norse sleipr from Proto-Germanic *slaipaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leyb-.
slab.g: A large, flat piece of solid material; a solid object that is large and flat.

slab.e: Acronym of Slow, Loud And Bangin'. This term been popularized through the southern rap genre of hip-hop, most notably by rappers such as Paul Wall, Chamillionaire, Lil' Keke, and others.
slab.g: A car that has been modified with equipment such as loudspeakers, lights, special paint, hydraulics, and other accessories.

slack.e: From Middle English slak, from Old English slæc (“slack”), from Proto-Germanic *slakaz. For sense of coal dust, compare slag.
slack.g: Lax; not tense; not firmly extended.

slacker.e: From slack + -er; compare especially slack off.
slacker.g: One who procrastinates or is lazy; one who does not do their fair share or pull their own weight.

slackness.e: From Middle English slacnesse, slakenes, slaknesse; equivalent to slack + -ness.
slackness.g: The state of being slack; the quality of having slack.

slam.e: From Middle English *slammen (not recorded), apparently from a Scandinavian source ultimately from Old Norse slæma, slœma (“to slam, swing a weapon, strike an object out of reach”), related to Old Norse slamra, slambra (“to slam”).
slam.g: To shut with sudden force so as to produce a shock and noise.

slam.e: Unknown and long-speculated, though perhaps at least reinforced by Etymology 1.
slam.g: A type of card game, also called ruff and honours.

slander.e: From Middle English slaundre, sclaundre, from Old French esclandre, from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum (“stumbling block, temptation”), from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon, “scandal”).
slander.g: A false or unsupported, malicious statement (spoken, not written), especially one which is injurious to a person's reputation; the making of

slanderer.g: One who slanders or defames the name or reputation of another person.

slanderously.g: In a slanderous manner; in a manner that causes slander; in a false and defamatory way.

slang.e: First use appears c. 1756, meaning "special vocabulary of tramps or thieves", origin unknown. Not believed to be connected with language or lingo.
slang.g: Language outside of conventional usage and in the informal register.

slang.e: The same as sling which is also used in this sense. The vowel exhibits the lowering of /ɪ/ before /ŋ/ distinguishing for African American Vernacular English, as in thang for thing, but the word has spread with this pronunciation outside the accents that exhibit this feature.

slap.e: From Middle English slappen, of uncertain origin, possibly imitative.
slap.g: A blow, especially one given with the open hand, or with something broad and flat.

slash.e: Late Middle English, originally a verb of uncertain etymology. Perhaps of imitative origin, or possibly from Old French esclachier (“to break in pieces”), a variant of esclater, which is likely a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *slaitan (“to slit, tear”). Used in the Wycliffe Bible as slascht (see 1 Kings 5:18) but otherwise unattested until 16th century.
Uncertain. Slang use for urination attested from the 1950s.
slash.g: A drink of something; a draft.

slaughter.e: From Middle English slaughter, from Old Norse *slahtr, later sláttr, from Proto-Germanic *slahtrą, from Proto-Germanic *slahaną. Equivalent to slay + -ter (as in laughter). Eventually derived from Proto-Indo-European *slak- (“to hit, strike, throw”). Related with Dutch slachten, German schlachten, Finnish lahdata (all “to slaughter”).
slaughter.g: The killing of animals, generally for food.

slave.e: From Middle English sclave, from Old French esclave, from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”), traditionally assumed to be because Slavs were often forced into slavery in the Middle Ages. The Latin word is from Medieval Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos); see that entry and Slav for more.
slave.g: A person who is held in servitude as the property of another person, and whose labor (and often also whose body and life) is subject to the

slay.e: From Middle English sleen, slen, from Old English slēan (“to hit, punch, strike; to kill”), from Proto-West Germanic *slahan, from Proto-Germanic *slahaną (“to hit, strike; to kill”), from Proto-Indo-European *slak- (“to hit, strike, throw”).

slayer.e: From Middle English slear, sleere, sleare, slaare, dissimilated from Old English slaga (“slayer”), equivalent to slay + -er.
slayer.g: A killer; a murderer; someone who slays.

sledge.e: From Middle English slegge, from Old English sleċġ (“sledgehammer; mallet”), from Proto-Germanic *slagjǭ.
Dialectal Dutch sleedse, from Middle Dutch sleedse, from the root of sled.
sledge.g: A low sled drawn by animals, typically on snow, ice or grass.

sleek.e: A late variant of slick; cognate to German schleichen (Old High German slihhan) and Dutch slijk (“mud, slime”).
sleek.g: Having an even, smooth surface; smooth

sleep.e: From Middle English slepen, from Anglian Old English slēpan (West Saxon Old English slǣpan), from Proto-West Germanic *slāpan, from Proto-Germanic *slēpaną (“to sleep”).
sleep.g: To rest in a state of reduced consciousness.

sleep.e: From Middle English slepe, sleep, sleepe, from Old English slǣp (“sleep”), from Proto-West Germanic *slāp, from Proto-Germanic *slēpaz (“sleep”).
sleep.g: The state of reduced consciousness during which a human or animal rests in a daily rhythm.

sleeper.e: From Middle English sleper, equivalent to sleep + -er.

sleepless.e: From Middle English slepeles, from Old English slǣplēas; equivalent to sleep + -less.
sleepless.g: Characterized by an absence of sleep: wakeful.

sleet.e: From Middle English slete, probably from Old English *slēte, *slȳte, *slīete, from Proto-West Germanic *slautijā, from Proto-Germanic *slautijǭ (“sleet”). Walter W. Skeat, the author of Etymological Dictionary of the English Language, suggests Old Norse slydda (whence Danish slud (“mixture of rain and snow”)).
sleet.g: Pellets of ice made of mostly-frozen raindrops or refrozen melted snowflakes.

sleight.e: From Middle English sleighte, sleyght, sleythe, from Old Norse slœgð (“cunning”), from Proto-Germanic *slōgiþō, from *slōgiz (“cunning”) (whence English sly).

slew.e: Ablaut of slay, from Middle English slew, sleugh, past of Middle English sleen. Replaced earlier Middle English slough, slogh, from Old English slōg (past of Old English slēan (“to hit, strike, slay”)), due to the influence of knew, drew, etc.

slice.e: From Middle English sclise, sklise, from Old French esclice, esclis (“a piece split off”), deverbal of esclicer, esclicier (“to splinter, split up”), from Frankish *slitjan (“to split up”), from Proto-Germanic *slitjaną, from Proto-Germanic *slītaną (“to split, tear apart”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyd- (“to rend, injure, crumble”).
slice.g: That which is thin and broad.

slick.e: From Middle English slicke, slike, slyke, from Old English slīc (“sleek, smooth; crafty, cunning, slick”), from Proto-Germanic *slīkaz (“sleek, smooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyg-, *sleyǵ- (“to glide, smooth, spread”).
slick.g: Slippery or smooth due to a covering of liquid; often used to describe appearances.

slide.e: From Middle English sliden, from Old English slīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *slīdan, from Proto-Germanic *slīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃sléydʰeti, from *h₃sleydʰ- (“slippery”) + *-eti.
slide.g: To (cause to) move in continuous contact with a surface.

slime.e: From Middle English slime, slyme, slim, slym, from Old English slīm, from Proto-West Germanic *slīm, from Proto-Germanic *slīmą, from Proto-Indo-European *sley- (“smooth; slick; sticky; slimy”). The slang sense of "to murder" spread among Black communites throughout the 2010s and gained prominence on TikTok around 2021.
slime.g: Soft, moist earth or clay, having an adhesive quality; viscous mud; any substance of a dirty nature, that is moist, soft, and adhesive; bitu

sling.e: From Middle English slynge (noun), slyngen (verb), probably from Old Norse slyngja, slyngva (“to hurl”), from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to worm, twist”) or compare Old English slingan (“to wind, twist”), from the same source.
sling.g: To throw with a circular or arcing motion.
A young or infant spider, such as one raised in captivity.

slinger.e: From Middle English slynger; equivalent to sling + -er.
slinger.g: Someone who, or something that, slings or uses a sling.

slingstone.g: A stone, bullet, or other such missile or projectile thrown by a sling.

slip.e: From Middle English slippen, probably from Middle Low German slippen, from Old Saxon *slippian, from Proto-West Germanic *slippjan, from Proto-Germanic *slipjaną (“to glide”), an iterative form of *slīpaną (“to slip, slide”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyb- (“slimy; to slide”).
slip.g: To lose one’s traction on a slippery surface; to slide due to a lack of friction.

slip.e: Probably from Middle Dutch slippe or Middle Low German slippe, probably ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *slīban (“to split”).
slip.g: A twig or shoot; a cutting.

slippery.e: From Middle English slipperie, an extended form ( + -y) of Middle English slipper, sliper (“slippery”), from Old English slipor (“slippery”), from Proto-Germanic *slipraz (“smooth, slippery”), equivalent to slip + -er.
slippery.g: Of a surface, having low friction, often due to being covered in a non-viscous liquid, and therefore hard to grip, hard to stand on without

slither.e: From Middle English slitheren, alteration of slideren (“to slither, creep”), from Old English slidrian (“to slip, slide, slither”), from Proto-West Germanic *slidrōn (“to slide, slither”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃sleydʰ- (“to slip”), equivalent to slide + -er (frequentative suffix).
slither.g: To move about smoothly and from side to side.

slope.g: A surface that either inclines or declines in a regular manner from the perspective of an observer.

slow.e: From Middle English slaw, slow, from Old English slāw (“lazy; inert, slow”), from Proto-West Germanic *slaiw, from Proto-Germanic *slaiwaz (“blunt; dull; exhausted, faint, sluggish, weak, weary; listless, torpid; dim-witted, slow; lazy, slack”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *sleyH-u- (“bad”).
slow.g: Taking a long time to move or go a short distance, or to perform an action; not quick in motion; proceeding at a low speed.

slowly.e: From Middle English slowly, slowli, slouli, slowliche, from Old English slāwlīċe (“slowly; sluggishly”), equivalent to slow + -ly.

slug.e: Originally referred to a slow, lazy person, from Middle English slugge (“lazy person", also "sloth, slothfulness”), probably of either Old English or Old Norse origin; perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sliǵ-ōn, from *sley- (“smooth; slick; sticky.
slug.g: Any of many gastropod mollusks, having no (or only a rudimentary) shell.

slug.e: Uncertain. Perhaps somehow from Proto-Germanic *slagiz (“a blow, strike”). If so, then cognate with slay and slaughter; also German Schlag (“blow, hit”) and Dutch slag (“blow, strike”).
slug.g: A hard blow, usually with the fist.

sluggard.e: From Middle English slogarde, probably ultimately of Old Norse origin. Equivalent to slug + -ard (“pejorative agent suffix”).
sluggard.g: A person who is lazy, stupid, or idle by habit.

sluice.e: From Middle English sluse, alteration of scluse, from Anglo-Norman escluse (“sluice, floodgate”), from Late Latin exclusa (“extrusion, gate”), from Latin exclūsus, form of exclūdō (“to shut out, to exclude”) (English exclude).
sluice.g: An artificial passage for water, fitted with a valve or gate, for example in a canal lock or a mill stream, for stopping or regulating the f

slumber.e: From Middle English slombren, slomren, frequentative of Middle English slummen, slumen (“to doze”), probably from Middle English slume (“slumber”), from Old English slūma, from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“slack, loose, limp, flabby”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lew- (“loose, limp, flabby”). By surface analysis, sloom + -er.
slumber.g: A very light state of sleep, almost awake.

slump.e: Probably of North Germanic origin: compare Danish slumpe (“to stumble upon by chance”), Norwegian slumpe (“happen by chance”), Norwegian slumpa (“happen by chance”), Swedish slumpa (“randomize; to sell off”), Swedish slump (“chance, randomness, happenstance”).
